newsitem.title: THAILAND: Cambodian fighting spurs flight to Thailand.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian fighting spurs flight to Thailand.

text.p: More than 20,000 Cambodian civilians fled into Thailand overnight to escape fighting in the besieged Cambodian town of O'Smach, Thai military officials said on Tuesday.

Thai authorities decided to open the gates at a checkpoint and allowed the civilians to walk across the border late on Monday after fighting between royalist troops holding the town and troops under Cambodian strongman Hun Sen moved closer to the centre of the town.
"There was the sound of heavy gunfire in the evening and we learned that Hun Sen troops overran Khao Laem," a Thai army officer told Reuters.
Khao Laem, a hill about five km (three miles) from O'Smach, was an important line of defence for the town's royalist defenders.
"Royalist troops are still in the town and the two sides are confronting each other just metres from each other," the Thai officer said.
Forces loyal to ousted Cambodian premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh have been fighting government troops under Hun Sen since shortly after the prince was ousted on July 6.
O'Smach, a town of more than 24,000 people, is the last stronghold of Ranariddh's troops.
A Khmer Rouge guerrilla helping the royalist troops said the fighting would intensify once civilians left the town.
"Once the civilians leave the fighters will not have to be concerned about their safety and then the fierce fighting will begin," the guerrilla told Reuters during a trip to O'Smach on Monday.
The refugees, most of them women and children, were allowed to seek temporary shelter at a border market about two km (one mile) inside Thailand.
Thai officials said the refugees would be transferred to a site prepared for them some seven km (four miles) from the border.
But some residents of the north Cambodian town refused to leave despite the approach of battle.
"Several hundred people are still in O'Smach. They said they wanted to stay there until the last minute," the Thai army officer said.
He said many Cambodians who fled to Thailand during the night had returned home early on Tuesday and found their homes had been looted in their absence.

About 9,000 Cambodians, mostly traders and their families, have been living in O'Smach for years. Other refugees who had been sheltering in the town were displaced from surrounding villages in recent weeks.
"We continue to live here even though Hun Sen troops are coming in, we can live with any faction, we're merchants not politicians," a Cambodian trader in O'Smach told Reuters late on Monday.
The Thai army has sent reinforcements into the area and sealed off the border as heavy fighting was expected in O'Smach later on Tuesday, the officer said.
